video.title: How to Get a Yes From Anyone (and Change Your Life)

summary: Stu Heinik discusses contact marketing: researching a small number of influential people and approaching them with a distinctive, personal campaign. Examples include a targeted Facebook ad that reportedly led a tongue-scraper startup to a Walmart order, a custom sword sent to struggling-company CEOs, and personalized cartoons and mail. Host Chris Koerner adds examples from his own businesses and pitches AI-assisted research and creative outreach. The central takeaway is to make a relevant approach memorable, then stay flexible about what the recipient needs.

speakers.name: Stu Heinik
speakers.description: Author of How to Get a Meeting with Anyone and practitioner of contact marketing.

ideas.name: Personalized contact marketing campaigns
ideas.one_liner: Create highly tailored campaigns to get a meeting with a small number of influential prospects.
ideas.business_model: Not stated; the guest describes creating campaigns for clients.
ideas.customer: Businesses or people seeking meetings with prospective clients, mentors, partners, or other influential decision-makers.
ideas.problem: Usual outreach channels can fail to attract attention from important prospects.
ideas.offer: Research a prospect and create a distinctive, personalized contact campaign, including cartoon mailings.

pricing.notes: The guest does not state what he charges clients.

acquisition_channels.details: Personalized cartoons were used in mailings. How the guest acquired paying clients is not stated.

quote.text: I wanted to use cartoons in those mailings. That's where it started.
quote.speaker: Stu Heinik

ideas.delivery: The guest describes personalized cartoon mailings and a group of skilled cartoonists. The cartoon is tailored to the recipient; a window in a FedEx envelope can reveal part of it and prompt the recipient to open the mailpiece. Human research and creative work are central.
unit_economics_claims: The guest says his first contact campaign achieved a 100% response rate.
The video introduction describes a campaign reaching about two dozen people, all of whom responded, met, and became clients.

acquisition.how: Software could help research prospects and prepare mailing lists, but selecting a small, high-value audience and creating relevant approaches requires human judgment. Physical mail is a possible UK-compliant channel, subject to data-protection rules.

onboarding.how: A form could collect target names and campaign goals, but a person would need to clarify the relationship, context, and appropriate tone.

delivery.how: Cartoon selection, personal research, and humor require substantial human creative work. Software could assist with research or production, but the guest stresses the distinctive work of practiced cartoonists.

billing.how: Invoicing and payment collection could be automated once a service and fee are agreed.

support.how: Routine status updates could be automated, but campaign changes and client feedback require human judgment.

uk_applicability.notes: Personalized mail and prospect research can work in the UK. The operator would need to handle personal data lawfully and respect direct-marketing rules.

risks: Personalization can take substantial time and skilled creative work.
Humor that disparages the recipient or gets details wrong can damage the approach; the guest advises keeping the recipient out of frame and making them come out well.
A memorable approach can earn a response without producing a sale or engagement.

quotes.text: A big feature of contact marketing is it's not mass marketing at all. It's finding the people like you know at the most 100 people
quotes.speaker: Stu Heinik

quotes.text: So, I didn't talk about it to anyone. I just thought, you know, it's be like saying I've been abducted by aliens
quotes.speaker: Stu Heinik

ideas.name: Tongue-scraper product sold online and through Walmart
ideas.one_liner: Sell a dentist-invented tongue scraper online and use a distinctive targeted ad to reach Walmart's dental-products buyer.
ideas.business_model: Physical product sales, with a large retailer order as a reported growth route.
ideas.customer: Consumers buying dental products and retail buyers such as Walmart's dental-products buyer.
ideas.problem: The transcript describes a tongue scraper and an ad saying Walmart employees have bad breath; it does not otherwise state the product's customer problem.
ideas.offer: A newly invented tongue scraper, sold online and pitched for rollout in Walmart stores.

pricing.model: Product sales; consumer price not stated.
pricing.notes: The ad cost and reported wholesale order are described, but the scraper's sale price is not.

acquisition_channels.details: The founders hired young people to make YouTube videos, which were reportedly selling the tongue scrapers effectively.

quote.text: A dentist had invented a new tongue scraper and so he started a company, hired some young guys to do videos for him on YouTube
quote.speaker: Stu Heinik

acquisition_channels.details: They paid for a static Facebook ad targeted at Walmart's Bentonville, Arkansas headquarters and used a humorous dental-product message. Walmart's legal department contacted them, then connected them with its dental-products buyer.

quote.text: They put together a little just a little tiny Facebook ad, static Facebook ad, paid $28 for it.
quote.speaker: Stu Heinik

ideas.delivery: The company made and sold a physical tongue scraper online. The reported Walmart order would distribute it through Walmart stores; manufacturing and fulfilment details are not stated.
unit_economics_claims: The company reportedly spent $28 on the Facebook ad and received a $2 million order.
The guest reports that the CEO estimated the company's valuation rose from $2 million to $20 million.
ideas.startup_cost: Not stated. The $28 Facebook ad was a campaign cost, not a stated total startup cost.

acquisition.how: Ad targeting, campaign delivery, and inbound lead capture can be automated. Creative development, compliance review, and retail-buyer relationship management still need human oversight.

onboarding.how: Online orders can be processed automatically. Retail onboarding, buyer negotiations, and product approval would need human involvement.

delivery.how: The product must be manufactured, packed, and physically shipped, so software cannot perform most delivery work.

billing.how: Online payments and invoices can be processed by ecommerce and accounting software; retailer terms may need human review.

support.how: Automated answers could handle routine order questions, with escalation for product and retailer issues.

uk_applicability.notes: The product and online-sales model could work in the UK, but the specific Walmart route and Bentonville targeting are US-specific. UK product, labelling, and retail requirements would need to be addressed.

risks: The reported order and valuation are second-hand claims from an interview, not independently verified figures.
The ad drew a response from Walmart's legal department; creative targeting and claims about a retailer's employees can create legal or reputational concerns.
A physical product requires manufacturing, stock, fulfilment, and retailer acceptance.

quotes.text: They put together a little just a little tiny Facebook ad, static Facebook ad, paid $28 for it.
quotes.speaker: Stu Heinik

quotes.text: And they exited that conversation with a 20, what was it? No, $2 million order.
quotes.speaker: Stu Heinik

ideas.name: Unofficial online store for Buc-ee's products
ideas.one_liner: Buy products from Buc-ee's stores and resell them online to customers who want the retailer's products.
ideas.customer: People who want Buc-ee's products online; the host says the company itself did not sell online.
ideas.problem: The host identified an online availability gap for products sold in Buc-ee's stores.
ideas.offer: An online business selling Buc-ee's products sourced from its physical stores; the host says it is unofficial and not an official partner.

pricing.model: Product sales; sale prices and margins are not stated.
pricing.notes: The host states the cost of an initial purchase but not customer prices.

acquisition_channels.details: The host bought products from stores, launched the business, and cold-emailed 20 reporters. He says the story went viral. For a UK operator, cold email rules depend on whether recipients are corporate subscribers or individuals/sole traders.

quote.text: It cost $1,500 and I launched a business and I cold emailed 20 reporters. It went viral.
quote.speaker: Chris Koerner

ideas.delivery: The host says the business sells Buc-ee's products online, but sourcing, packing, shipping, and customer support processes are not described.
unit_economics_claims: The host says the initial purchase cost $1,500.
The host says the business does millions of dollars a year in sales.
ideas.startup_cost: The host says he spent $1,500 buying one of everything from the stores; other startup costs are not stated.

acquisition.how: The host's initial press outreach was manual. Store traffic or online advertising could be automated, but UK cold email to individuals and sole traders requires consent; B2B rules and screening apply.

onboarding.how: An ecommerce site can automatically take orders and collect shipping details.

delivery.how: Products must be sourced, stocked, packed, and shipped physically.

billing.how: An online store can automate payment and order records.

support.how: Automated answers can handle routine order questions, but sourcing, returns, and delivery exceptions need human handling.

uk_applicability.notes: Online resale is a portable model, but Buc-ee's is a US retailer and the host describes an unofficial relationship. A UK version would need a local product source and careful review of brand, resale, and cross-border shipping issues.

risks: The host says the business is not an official partner; brand permissions and retailer objections could affect the model.
The account depends on sourcing and shipping physical products.
The host's reported sales are not accompanied by costs, margins, or independent verification.

quotes.text: I bought one of everything from their stores. It cost $1,500 and I launched a business and I cold emailed 20 reporters.
quotes.speaker: Chris Koerner

quotes.text: we do millions of dollars a year and we sell all of Buckyy's products online unofficially.

ideas.name: Commercial real estate brokerage through personalized outreach
ideas.one_liner: Use a framed local-news clipping and personal note to win a small-business owner as a commercial real estate client.
ideas.customer: Small-business owners opening or leasing retail locations.
ideas.problem: A business owner opening a location needs commercial real estate help; the transcript does not state other customer problems.
ideas.offer: Commercial real estate services and help finding a location for the owner's next store.

pricing.model: Commission described as a percentage of the lease value.
pricing.notes: The host describes a $3,000 monthly rent, a five-year lease, and a 5% commission. The figures are the host's estimate of the broker's value.

acquisition_channels.details: A commercial realtor found the host's new lease through tax records or another source, used a local newspaper article, laminated and framed it, and added a note offering to help find his next store.

quote.text: he had taken that paper and laminated it and like framed it and he put a note in there
quote.speaker: Chris Koerner

ideas.delivery: The broker would help the client find a commercial location and arrange a lease. The transcript does not detail the brokerage's service process.
unit_economics_claims: The host estimates that the broker spent half an hour and $10 in materials to win a commission worth $9,000.
ideas.startup_cost: The host says the outreach materials cost $10; other startup costs are not stated.

acquisition.how: Finding a trigger and preparing a personalized physical mailpiece is mostly human work. Public-record research can be supported by software, subject to data and marketing rules.

onboarding.how: Forms and scheduling can be automated, but client needs and property requirements require human discussion.

delivery.how: Commercial property search, negotiation, and lease support depend on human brokerage work.

billing.how: Commission invoicing can be automated after the deal terms are known.

support.how: Clients need human support during property search and negotiation.

uk_applicability.notes: Commercial brokerage and personalized post can work in the UK. Commission practices, lease terms, data sources, and applicable property rules vary.

risks: The commission calculation is the host's estimate, not a verified statement from the realtor.
Lease sourcing and negotiation are relationship-driven and require human work.

quotes.text: He spent half hour of his time, $10 in materials to hand deliver that to me for $9,000.
quotes.speaker: Chris Koerner

ideas.name: Turnaround advisory for struggling companies
ideas.one_liner: Identify companies missing earnings estimates, send the CEO a personalized sword, and offer help improving results.
ideas.business_model: Turnaround work with compensation described tentatively as a stake in results.
ideas.customer: CEOs of companies in trouble, including businesses with missed earnings estimates.
ideas.problem: A company is struggling or has recently missed earnings estimates.
ideas.offer: Turnaround assistance, introduced with a custom sword inscribed with the CEO's name and a handwritten note.

pricing.model: The guest says he thinks compensation is a stake in the results produced; the exact arrangement is not known.
pricing.notes: A flat fee or equity terms are not stated. The guest explicitly says he does not know the compensation structure.

acquisition_channels.details: Dan Walshmitt scans business news each morning for missed earnings estimates, then sends the CEO a custom sword in a presentation box with a handwritten note. The transcript also mentions follow-up outreach, but gives no detailed sequence.

quote.text: the way that he went about first of all finding them and then contacting the CEOs was he scan the business news every morning looking for stories of missed earnings estimates.
quote.speaker: Stu Heinik

ideas.delivery: A turnaround specialist works with the company to improve results. The transcript does not describe the consulting process. The sword is a physical prospecting gift, not the service delivery.
unit_economics_claims: The custom sword costs about $1,000 to make.
The guest says responses to the campaign have been 100%, and engagements are worth a million dollars and up.
tools: Custom sword from a propmaker associated with the movie Gladiator
ideas.startup_cost: A custom sword costs about $1,000; other startup costs are not stated.

acquisition.how: News monitoring could be automated, but choosing targets, commissioning a personalized gift, and following up require human review and substantial manual work. UK cold calls to relevant business numbers must be screened against TPS/CTPS where applicable.

onboarding.how: A CEO's situation and potential engagement need human discussion and due diligence.

delivery.how: Turnaround consulting involves diagnosing and changing a real business; humans must do the work.

billing.how: Invoicing can be automated, but a results-based or equity-linked agreement needs human negotiation and review.

support.how: Company leadership and turnaround support require ongoing human involvement.

uk_applicability.notes: Turnaround consulting and business-news research apply in the UK, but the prospecting trigger, gift costs, company context, and follow-up practices would need adapting. The sword example is expensive and highly personal.

risks: The guest is unsure about the specialist's compensation model and does not verify the number or value of resulting engagements.
A $1,000 gift is an expensive acquisition cost and corporate gift policies may limit its acceptability.
The sword approach and any follow-up may not work for every CEO or company.

quotes.text: And then he has this sword made up, this beautiful sword made by the propmaker for the movie Gladiator.
quotes.speaker: Stu Heinik

quotes.text: If you're not all in, you're not in at all.
quotes.speaker: Stu Heinik

ideas.name: Instagram Reels performance analysis service
ideas.one_liner: Analyze creators' video retention data and recommend changes to improve hooks and performance.
ideas.business_model: Freelance or short-term service work; the host suggests a paid trial but states no exact fee.
ideas.customer: Creators or businesses publishing Instagram Reels.
ideas.problem: A video may have weak performance despite having a strong swipe-away rate or other useful retention signal.
ideas.offer: Review Reels data, identify promising hooks, and recommend changes or refilming.

pricing.model: Paid trial suggested by the host; exact rate not stated.
pricing.notes: The host says he would pay above market for a 30-day trial, but gives no amount.

acquisition_channels.details: A prospective analyst sent the host money through Venmo with a note offering to help film content. The host later contacted him about a different need. UK rules restrict unsolicited marketing messages to individuals and sole traders; a payment note is not a safe substitute for consent.

quote.text: And in the comments, in in the name of the transaction, he said, "Read the comments," which no one reads Venmo comments unless you point to it.
quote.speaker: Chris Koerner

ideas.delivery: The analyst would review Instagram Reels swipe-away rates, identify strong hooks, and recommend content changes. The host describes a potential 30-day trial producing 30 videos, but no work was actually agreed in the transcript.
unit_economics_claims: The host proposes a 30-day trial and about 30 videos, with above-market pay but no stated amount.

acquisition.how: The example depends on a personal, unsolicited approach. In the UK, do not automate unsolicited marketing messages to individuals or sole traders without consent; inbound referrals and permission-based channels would be more suitable.

onboarding.how: A structured intake could gather account access and goals, with a human agreeing scope and permissions.

delivery.how: Software can collect performance data and flag patterns, but interpreting creative context and recommending changes need human judgment.

billing.how: A defined subscription or trial could use automated invoicing and payments.

support.how: Routine report delivery can be automated, but feedback and creative recommendations require human discussion.

uk_applicability.notes: Creator analytics work is applicable in the UK and Instagram is available. The unsolicited payment-note acquisition method is not a suitable default under UK marketing rules.

risks: The prospect's approach initially offered camera work, while the host later had a different need; offers can miss the customer's immediate requirement.
The prospect failed to follow up after the host did not respond, then asked about a long-term role before a trial.
The service depends on access to platform analytics and a human who can interpret content performance.

quotes.text: I need someone to just kind of be a data analyst that knows how to read the trends like someone who has a mind for it
quotes.speaker: Chris Koerner

ideas.name: AI-assisted personalized prospect research and outreach
ideas.one_liner: Use AI to research a prospect's interests and personalize outreach at scale, while keeping the approach distinctive and relevant.
ideas.business_model: Not stated; presented as a possible marketing capability or service.
ideas.customer: Businesses or individuals trying to reach a specific influential prospect or small list of decision-makers.
ideas.problem: Generic approaches fail to stand out, while manual research and personalization can take time.
ideas.offer: Use AI-assisted dossier research to find a personal interest or contextual detail, then adapt a campaign or creative asset for the recipient.

pricing.notes: The host pitches AI-assisted personalization but does not describe a paid offer or price.

acquisition_channels.details: The host suggests making a cartoon and using AI to customize variables for recipients. He also describes researching a public social-media handle and using a distinctive interest as an outreach angle.

quote.text: That is one thing that AI could do very well is you hand make a cartoon and but you have AI plug in thousands or hundreds or dozens of different variables that make it custom to each person you're sending it to.
quote.speaker: Chris Koerner

ideas.delivery: AI could gather public information, summarize a prospect dossier, and adapt selected campaign details. The host proposes human-made creative with AI-assisted customization; fully automated cartoon quality is not demonstrated.

acquisition.how: Agents can research prospects and prepare drafts, but a person should check relevance, accuracy, and the legal basis before contact. UK direct marketing restrictions apply to unsolicited electronic outreach.

onboarding.how: A client could submit target criteria and campaign goals through a form, with human review of the brief.

delivery.how: Agents can find public context and customize approved variables, while a human checks factual accuracy, tone, and creative quality.

billing.how: Recurring or campaign fees could be invoiced automatically if a commercial model were defined.

support.how: Automated updates could cover campaign status, but clients may need human review of sensitive personalization decisions.

uk_applicability.notes: AI research and personalized marketing are usable in the UK, but personal-data processing and PECR rules must be followed. Physical direct mail and consent-based or compliant business outreach are safer channels than unsolicited messages to individuals.

risks: The transcript does not demonstrate that AI can consistently make cartoons as compelling as skilled human cartoonists.
Public research can surface stale, irrelevant, or sensitive personal information.
Automated personalization can become intrusive or inaccurate if a person does not review it.

quotes.text: one of the uses that would be interesting is to just have dossier produced let people really quickly find some handle something that they they love to do
quotes.speaker: Stu Heinik

ideas.problem: A conventional application may not stand out, and candidates may fear looking foolish by making an unusual approach.
ideas.offer: A resume delivered with a memorable, personalized gesture or story.

pricing.notes: The examples are job-seeking tactics, not paid products.

acquisition_channels.details: Examples include bringing a box of donuts with a resume or delivering an empty, donut-stained box with a note about having eaten the donuts while waiting for a deal.

acquisition.how: The method depends on a candidate physically approaching an employer; the transcript's examples require a human to carry and deliver the item.

onboarding.how: The employer and candidate must communicate directly about the role.

delivery.how: The candidate must make the physical presentation in person.

billing.how: No paid service or billing process is described.

support.how: Any interview or hiring process involves direct human interaction.

uk_applicability.notes: A creative job application can work in the UK, but employers' access policies and workplace norms vary. In-person delivery requires the candidate to attend.

risks: The unusual approach may not suit every employer or role.
The transcript gives no outcome data for the donut-box examples.

tactics.name: Focus on a short list of high-impact prospects
steps: Define the outcome you want, such as a client, mentor, or partner.
Build a small list of people who could materially change the outcome.
Spend time researching and approaching that list rather than defaulting to a large generic campaign.

quote.text: what happened if we took 5 hours trying to reach like the 20 most influential people that could completely transform our business?
quote.speaker: Chris Koerner

tactics.name: Make outreach specific to the recipient
steps: Research the recipient's public interests and current context.
Choose a relevant detail that makes the approach feel specific to them.
Make the recipient come out well in any humor or creative work.

quote.text: So, the cartoon always going to be about the recipient. And because of what cartoons do in magazines and newspapers anyway
quote.speaker: Stu Heinik

tactics.name: Use a physical teaser to make the recipient open the mail
steps: Show only part of a compelling image through a cutout window in the envelope.
Place the full creative inside so the recipient has to open the package to see the payoff.
Use the rest of the mailpiece to continue the story or offer.

quote.text: it's a method for using cartoons to get people to pay attention whatever it is that you sent, whether it's a mailpiece or an FedEx envelope
quote.speaker: Stu Heinik

tactics.name: Target a buyer's headquarters with a memorable ad
steps: Identify the location and likely audience of the decision-maker you need to reach.
Run a small, narrowly targeted ad with a distinctive creative idea.
If the organization responds through legal or communications staff, cooperate with requests and explain the targeting.
Use the conversation to ask for an introduction to the relevant buyer.

tactics.name: Find turnaround prospects through business news
steps: Review business news regularly for companies missing earnings estimates.
Research the CEO and the company's situation before approaching.
Use a personalized item and handwritten note that connects the company's setback to the service offered.
Follow up as needed and be ready to explain a relevant way to help.

tactics.name: Follow up by referencing the original approach and the prospect's current need
steps: Refer back to the distinctive first contact so the recipient remembers why you reached out.
Ask what help they need now instead of assuming the original offer still fits.
Offer a small, time-limited paid trial before discussing a long-term role or relationship.

steps: Research whether a relevant buyer or decision-maker is involved in a local community activity.

warnings.warning: A high response rate does not mean every recipient engages, buys, or becomes a client; the guest distinguishes response from engagement.
Do not use humor that disparages the prospect or relies on details that may be wrong. The guest says the recipient should come out well and stay out of frame.
The custom sword campaign has a reported cost of about $1,000 per prospect, and its compensation model and results are not fully established in the transcript.

The host's Venmo example shows that an unusual opening can get attention, but the prospect did not follow up after the host failed to respond and later asked about a long-term role before agreeing a trial.

For UK outreach, unsolicited marketing email, SMS, WhatsApp, and social DMs to individuals and sole traders require consent under the user's stated PECR rule. Cold email to limited companies can be allowed, and cold calls must be screened against TPS/CTPS.
The host's reported online sales, the Walmart order and valuation, the realtor commission, and the sword campaign results are speaker claims, not independently verified figures.

evidence_quality.rationale: The guest explains a specific contact-marketing process and gives a first-person campaign example, but many of the strongest business outcomes are anecdotes reported from third parties and cannot be checked from the transcript. Costs, sales, response rates, and valuations are speaker claims with limited context.
evidence_quality.promotional_conflict: Stu Heinik is promoting his book How to Get a Meeting with Anyone and its new edition. The transcript also contains the host promoting his own podcast and newsletter.
